item.title: Viewer dossier, a seven-day curse and subscriptions
item.description: A dossier with your stats and lists, a Watch-the-video mode with a call a week later, whispers and creaks in reviews and in the room, an email sign-up and RSS. Every review and feature now has its own page.

item.title: More films and reviews
item.description: The catalogue gained 23 films and 29 new reviews were written, from Caligari and Häxan to Sinners and Weapons. Three more lead reviews: Ringu, Suspiria and The Thing.

item.title: New feature: the video store and VHS
item.description: A long read on how tapes, rental shelves and the British “video nasties” list created the cult of hard-edged cinema. Find it in the Feature section.

item.title: Nine new touches
item.description: The moon phase, a REC counter, fogged glass, a 3 a.m. call, a spirit board, find-the-ghost, a fear map and a 404 page. Some of them hide until the right moment.

item.title: Sound of The Tape
item.description: The Tape clip has a new audio track: whispers, scrapes, static and drops into silence. Best with headphones.

item.title: A site for every subgenre
item.description: The Franchises section now has eight worlds: Slashers, Giallo, Body horror and Splatter joined Ringu, Ju-On, Ito and Tomie. Reviews are mixed across genres and the front page is about horror as a whole again.

item.title: November and December releases
item.description: Ten films with release dates were added to the New section, from Godzilla Minus Zero to Eggers’ Werwulf. Dates come from public roundups, so check them before you go to the cinema or stream.

item.title: Brighter and simpler
item.description: New visitors now start with the clean tone so the text is easier to read. The tone changes with the button at the top. The Telegram link is gone and a few more films were added.

item.title: The four pillars of the site
item.description: Ringu, Ju-On, Junji Ito and Tomie now have their own section, franchise filters, a dozen new films and three reviews.

item.title: Share buttons
item.description: Every review now has VK and copy buttons so you can share your finds.

item.title: The catalogue: nearly six hundred films
item.description: We added almost 300 new films: 30s–60s classics, forgotten slashers, giallo, European gothic, Asian cinema and the fresh wave. Fourteen new lists and 36 new reviews are up.

item.title: Visit streak and badges
item.description: Come back daily: the streak unlocks badges. One of them is secret. Progress is stored in your browser.

item.title: A new header and a flashlight
item.description: The header banners now rotate, and the Flashlight button kills the lights and leaves only a circle around your cursor.

item.title: The gallery grows to 37 works
item.description: The gallery has new posters, banners and logos. Open an image and flip through with the arrow keys.

item.title: New feature: J-Horror Trash
item.description: A long read on how Japanese horror turned into a carnival of blood and self-irony. Find it in the Feature section.

item.title: Newcomers: three routes into the genre
item.description: A new section collects routes through splatter, body horror and slashers: five films each, in order of rising gore.

item.title: The catalogue grows: nearly three hundred films
item.description: The catalogue now holds nearly three hundred films, from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) to fresh hits. Search by title or year.

item.title: Giallo for newcomers: three steps
item.description: Start with The Bird with the Crystal Plumage, then Deep Red, and only then Suspiria. This way it is easier to see how style outgrows plot.

item.title: J-Horror and J-Trash: two shelves
item.description: If tonight calls for ghosts, take Ringu and Ju-On. If it calls for blood and madness, Tokyo Gore Police and The Machine Girl.

item.title: Extreme without surprises
item.description: Before a heavy film check the warning in the list. We mark the hardest titles with a badge and say what to expect.

item.title: Practical versus CGI
item.description: Want to see how blood was made without a computer? Rewatch The Thing, Re-Animator and Braindead.

item.title: Trash night: the viewing order
item.description: For a group: The Toxic Avenger, then Troll 2, then Sharknado. Each one is more absurd than the last.

item.title: Grindhouse 101
item.description: The basics of exploitation: Last House on the Left, Death Race 2000 and Planet Terror as a modern tribute.

item.title: New section: subgenres
item.description: Folk horror, found footage, zombies, vampires, cannibals and seven more directions: each with its own set of films.

item.title: Halloween night: five films in a row
item.description: My marathon for tonight runs from Evil Dead II to Martyrs. See the full order in the shelves below.

item.title: Evil Dead Burn: what to rewatch first
item.description: The film came out on 10 July. If you have not seen the originals, start with Evil Dead II: it sets the tone of the series fastest.

item.title: Clayface and The Fly: how to watch body horror
item.description: If you liked Clayface, compare it with The Fly and The Thing: the same fears of one's own body, in a different tone.

item.title: Camp Miasma and the camp slashers
item.description: The summer's meta-slasher came out on 7 August. To prepare: Friday the 13th, Sleepaway Camp and The Burning in our shelf “Summer, camp, knife”.

item.title: Clayface hits cinemas
item.description: James Watkins' film came out on 23 October and is already being called the fall's most bodily horror film. A review will follow after I see it.

item.title: Eggers prepares a Christmas Werwulf
item.description: Robert Eggers' new werewolf film arrives on 25 December. It is a dark medieval story with transformation at its centre.

item.title: J-Horror Trash: when Japanese horror laughs at itself
item.description: While the world feared long-haired ghosts in wells, another Japanese cinema played in the next theatre: fountains of blood, weapons in place of arms and directors who apologised to no one.

item.title: Video nasties: how tapes made horror a mass hobby
item.description: In the early 1980s British newspapers declared war on tapes of hard-edged films. The war ended in a list of bans that made those films legends.
